General additive modeling evaluated factors potentially modulating performance (age, sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and pubertal developmental stage).Older no/low-drinking participants achieved better scores than younger ones on 5 accuracy composites (general ability, abstraction, attention, emotion, and balance). Speeded responses for attention, motor speed, and general ability were sensitive to age and pubertal development. The exceeds-threshold group (accounting for age, sex, and other demographic factors) performed significantly below the no/low-drinking group on balance accuracy and on general ability, attention, episodic memory, emotion, and motor speed scores and showed evidence for faster speed at the expense of accuracy. Delay Discounting performance was consistent with poor impulse control in the younger no/low drinkers and in exceeds-threshold drinkers regardless of age.Higher achievement with older age and pubertal stage in general ability, abstraction, attention, emotion, and balance suggests continued functional development through adolescence, possibly supported by concurrently maturing frontal, limbic, and cerebellar brain systems. Determination of whether low scores by the exceeds-threshold group resulted from drinking or from other preexisting factors requires longitudinal study. (PsycINFO Database Record", 
"Abstract Background The Identifying Child Anxiety Through Schools-identification to intervention (iCATS-i2i) trial is being conducted to establish whether ‘screening and intervention’, consisting of usual school practice plus a pathway comprising screening, feedback and a brief parent-led online intervention (OSI: Online Support and Intervention for child anxiety), bring clinical and health economic benefits compared to usual school practice and assessment only — ‘usual school practice’, for children aged 8–9 years in the following: (1) the ‘target population’, who initially screen positive for anxiety problems according to a two-item parent-report child anxiety questionnaire — iCATS-2, and (2) the ‘total population’, comprising all children in participating classes. This article describes the detailed statistical analysis plan for the trial. Methods and design iCATS-i2i is a definitive, superiority, pragmatic, school-based cluster randomised controlled trial (with internal pilot), with two parallel groups. Schools are randomised 1:1 to receive either screening and intervention or usual school practice. This article describes the following: trial objectives and outcomes; statistical analysis principles, including detailed estimand information necessary for aligning trial objectives, conduct, analyses and interpretation when there are different analysis populations and outcome measures to be considered; and planned main analyses, sensitivity and additional analyses. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov ISRCTN76119074. Registered on 4 January 2022", 
"Although genetic variation is a major risk factor of neurodevelopmental disorders, environmental factors during pregnancy and early life are also important in disease expression. Animal models demonstrate that maternal inflammation causes fetal neuroinflammation and neurodevelopmental deficits, and brain transcriptomics of neurodevelopmental disorders in humans show upregulated differentially expressed genes are enriched in immune pathways. We prospectively recruited 200 sequentially referred children with tic disorders/obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), 100 autoimmune neurological controls, and 100 age-matched healthy controls. A structured interview captured the maternal and family history of autoimmune disease and other pro-inflammatory states. Maternal blood and published Tourette brain transcriptomes were analysed for overlapping enriched pathways. Mothers of children with tics/OCD had a higher rate of autoimmune disease compared with mothers of children with autoimmune neurological conditions (p = 0.054), and mothers of healthy controls (p = 0.0004). Autoimmunity was similarly elevated in first- and second-degree maternal relatives of children with tics/OCD (p < 0.0001 and p = 0.014 respectively). Other pro-inflammatory states were also more common in mothers of children with tics/OCD than controls (p < 0.0001). Upregulated differentially expressed genes in maternal autoimmune disease and Tourette brain transcriptomes were commonly enriched in innate immune processes. Pro-inflammatory states, including autoimmune disease, are more common in the mothers and families of children with tics/OCD. Exploratory transcriptome analysis indicates innate immune signalling may link maternal inflammation and childhood tics/OCD. Targeting inflammation may represent preventative strategies in pregnancy and treatment opportunities for children with neurodevelopmental disorders.", 
"The symptom heterogeneity of schizophrenia is consistent with Wittgenstein's analogy of a language game. From the perspective of precision medicine, this study aimed to estimate the symptom presentation and identify the psychonectome in Asian patients, using data obtained from the Research on Asian Psychotropic Prescription Patterns for Antipsychotics. We constructed a network structure of the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) items in 1438 Asian patients with schizophrenia. Furthermore, all the BPRS items were considered to be an ordered categorical variable ranging in value from 1-7. Motor retardation was situated most centrally within the BPRS network structure, followed by depressive mood and unusual thought content. Contrastingly, hallucinatory behavior was situated least centrally within the network structure. Using a community detection algorithm, the BPRS items were organized into positive, negative, and general symptom clusters. Overall, DSM symptoms were not more central than non-DSM symptoms within the symptom network of Asian patients with schizophrenia. Thus, motor retardation, which results from the unmet needs associated with current antipsychotic medications for schizophrenia, may be a tailored treatment target for Asian patients with schizophrenia. Based on these findings, targeting non-dopamine systems (glutamate, γ-aminobutyric acid) may represent an effective strategy with respect to precision medicine for psychosis.", 
"Background Crisis resolution teams (CRTs) offer brief, intensive home treatment for people experiencing mental health crisis. CRT implementation is highly variable; positive trial outcomes have not been reproduced in scaled-up CRT care. Aims To evaluate a 1-year programme to improve CRTs’ model fidelity in a non-masked, cluster-randomised trial (part of the Crisis team Optimisation and RElapse prevention (CORE) research programme, trial registration number: ISRCTN47185233). Method Fifteen CRTs in England received an intervention, informed by the US Implementing Evidence-Based Practice project, involving support from a CRT facilitator, online implementation resources and regular team fidelity reviews. Ten control CRTs received no additional support. The primary outcome was patient satisfaction, measured by the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ-8), completed by 15 patients per team at CRT discharge ( n = 375). Secondary outcomes: CRT model fidelity, continuity of care, staff well-being, in-patient admissions and bed use and CRT readmissions were also evaluated. Results All CRTs were retained in the trial. Median follow-up CSQ-8 score was 28 in each group: the adjusted average in the intervention group was higher than in the control group by 0.97 (95% CI −1.02 to 2.97) but this was not significant ( P = 0.34). There were fewer in-patient admissions, lower in-patient bed use and better staff psychological health in intervention teams. Model fidelity rose in most intervention teams and was significantly higher than in control teams at follow-up. There were no significant effects for other outcomes. Conclusions The CRT service improvement programme did not achieve its primary aim of improving patient satisfaction. It showed some promise in improving CRT model fidelity and reducing acute in-patient admissions.", 
"The growing interest in scientometry stems from ethical concerns related to the proper evaluation of scientific contributions of an author working in a hard science. In the absence of a consensus, institutions may use arbitrary methods for evaluating scientists for employment and promotion. There are several indices in use that attempt to establish the most appropriate and suggestive position of any scientist in the field he/she works in. A scientist's Hirsch-index (h-index) quantifies their total effective published output, but h-index summarizes the total value of their published work without regard to their contribution to each publication. Consequently, articles where the author was a primary contributor carry the same weight as articles where the author played a minor role. Thus, we propose an updated h-index named Hirsch(p,t)-index that informs about both total scientific output and output where the author played a primary role. Our measure, h(p,t) = h(p),h(t), is composed of the h-index h(t) and the h-index calculated for articles where the author was a key contributor; i.e. first/shared first or senior or corresponding author. Thus, a h(p,t) = 5,10 would mean that the author has 5 articles as first, shared first, senior or corresponding author with at least 5 citations each, and 10 total articles with at least 10 citations each. This index can be applied in biomedical disciplines and in all areas where the first and last position on an article are the most important. Although other indexes, such as r- and w-indexes, were proposed for measuring the authors output based on the position of researchers within the published articles, our simpler strategy uses the already established algorithms for h-index calculation and may be more practical to implement.", 
"Abstract Contemporary theories propose that dysregulation of emotional perception is involved in the aetiology of psychosis. 298 healthy adolescents were assessed at age 14- and 19-years using fMRI while performing a facial emotion task. Psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) were assessed with the CAPE-42 questionnaire at age 19. The high PLEs group at age 19 years exhibited an enhanced response in right insular cortex and decreased response in right prefrontal, right parahippocampal and left striatal regions; also, a gradient of decreasing response to emotional faces with age, from 14 to 19 years, in the right parahippocampal region and left insular cortical area. The right insula demonstrated an increasing response to emotional faces with increasing age in the low PLEs group, and a decreasing response over time in the high PLEs group. The change in parahippocampal/amygdala and insula responses during the perception of emotional faces in adolescents with high PLEs between the ages of 14 and 19 suggests a potential ‘aberrant’ neurodevelopmental trajectory for critical limbic areas. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 133 columns across 14 data files.
#### Issues Identified

27 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 14 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Purpose
We aim to evaluate the factorial structure and psychometric properties of the MWLCS with Spanish normal weight, overweight and obese samples.

Methods
The research was carried out in two different studies. The first included a sample of 140 normal weight participants, selected out of a 274 sample recruited with an online survey. Study 2 was carried out in a sample of 633 participants recruited from the PREDIMED-Plus study. Out of them, 558 participants fulfilled the weight criteria and were categorized into: overweight (BMI 25 − < 29.99; N = 170), obese class I (BMI 30 − < 34.99; N = 266), and obese class II (BMI 35 − < 39.99; N = 122). Exploratory (EFA) and confirmatory (CFA) factor analyses were used to evaluate the factor structure of the MWLCS, and reliabilities and Spearman’s correlations were estimated. Invariance measurement was tested across the three subgroups of weight in Study 2.

Results
A three-factor structure indicating weight locus of control factors (internal, chance, and powerful others) was supported, both via EFA in the normal weight sample and CFA in the overweight and obese samples. In the normal weight sample, the powerful others dimension was positively related to BMI and the dimensions of the Dutch Eating Behaviors Questionnaire. Additionally, the scale showed evidence of scalar invariance across the groups with different weight conditions.

Conclusions
This scale seems to be a psychometrically appropriate instrument and its use is highly recommended when designing interventions for overweight or obese individuals."

#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 15 scripts: 1 ran without error, 13 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script needs a person** to choose a file, answer a question or use an app, which cannot be reproduced without one: 01_retrieve_data_from_snapshot.R. text.text: To increase coordination in areas of science where collaboration can benefit knowledge generation, collaborative work must also provide incentives for individual researchers to participate.
This study investigates the reasons for forming large-team collaborations and the individual-level outcomes associated with participating in these projects in psychology.

Through a qualitative analysis of 500 papers, we find that large-team collaborations are most often formed to address practical challenges inherent in complex research questions, although they can also serve broader social or strategic functions.

A quantitative analysis of 1,699,489 papers published between 1975 and 2024 shows that large-team papers receive more citations and are published in journals with greater citation prestige than smaller-team papers.
Large-team papers also receive more citations within the first two years after publication, indicating greater early citation impact.
These differences are also apparent within individual researchers' publication records, with their larger-team papers tending to receive more citations than their smaller-team papers.

Overall, our findings suggest that large-team collaboration can help researchers address the resource and coordination demands of complex research while also being associated with publication and citation outcomes that are currently rewarded within academia.
Science increasingly faces questions for which individual teams are poorly equipped (Klug & Bagrow, 2016; Leahey, 2016).

text.text: To successfully address these questions, researchers need to coordinate to manage interdependencies, whether temporal, logistic, financial, or epistemic (Rasti et al., 2026).

text.text: In many fields, coordination has emerged in what is referred to as large-team collaboration, which can provide researchers with access to a larger pool of resources, such as funding, human resources, complementary skills, and social capital (Lee et al., 2015).

text.text: Several of these long-term coordinated research efforts have led to impressive scientific progress, from the discovery of the Higgs Boson at CERN (European Council for Nuclear Research, Aad et al., 2012), to a consistent focus on patient-reported outcomes in rheumatology at OMERACT (Outcome Measures in Rheumatology, Tugwell et al., 2007), and complete and accurate modelling of the climate system at WCRP (World Climate Research Programme, Sommeria & Touzé-Peiffer, 2019).

text.text: Psychology has also increasingly adopted such collaborative approaches, particularly following large-scale replication initiatives such as Many Labs and the Reproducibility Project: Psychology (Klein et al., 2014; Open Science Collaboration, 2015).

text.text: Yet the collective epistemic benefits of coordination do not necessarily imply that participating in large-team science is beneficial to individual researchers.
This distinction is important as the current reward structure in academia places considerable weight on traditional metrics such as citation counts and the prestige of the journal.
The use of these metrics as indicators of scientific quality (Aksnes et al., 2019) and metrics worthy of reward and recognition (Declaration on Research Assessment, 2012) has been challenged.
text.formatted: The use of these metrics as indicators of scientific quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Aksnes et al., 2019)</ref> and metrics worthy of reward and recognition (Declaration on Research Assessment, 2012) has been challenged.

text.text: Yet, they still can influence decisions about hiring, promotion, funding, and professional recognition.

This poses a challenge for the uptake of coordinated projects, as they require researchers to invest scarce time, expertise, and resources, while potentially reducing autonomy and distributing scientific credit among a larger number of co-authors.

Sustaining large-scale coordination may therefore depend partly on whether these investments also generate benefits on metrics that are currently rewarded for the careers of researchers who make these contributions.
Existing research provides only partial answers to these questions.

A growing body of literature shows that, across different fields, papers produced by larger teams tend to receive more citations (Bikard et al., 2015; Hsiehchen et al., 2015; Larivière et al., 2015; Porter et al., 2012; Uzzi et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2019; Wuchty et al., 2007).

This pattern has also been observed in psychology, where large-team papers receive more citations and greater attention from news outlets and social media than papers with fewer authors (Coles, 2024; Coles et al., 2026). text.text: This leaves open the question whether the citation advantage associated with larger teams is also apparent within individual researchers' publication records and how citation outcomes vary across the broader distribution of team sizes.

Beyond the question on social benefits of large-team papers, an outstanding question is how epistemic reasons for large-team collaborations (i.e., different interdependencies) are visible in the papers produced by them.

For example, do people collaborate to perform expensive projects, collect data that is logistically impossible in a smaller team, or do they examine questions that require more expertise than a single person can acquire?

Jones (2021) reported that teams benefit from more diverse expertise and more creative idea combinations. Iglič et al. (2017), by surveying Slovenian researchers, reported that pooling resources and requiring more diverse expertise are among the reasons that promote collaborations.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Jones (2021)</ref> reported that teams benefit from more diverse expertise and more creative idea combinations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Iglič et al. (2017)</ref>, by surveying Slovenian researchers, reported that pooling resources and requiring more diverse expertise are among the reasons that promote collaborations.

text.text: Yet, we do not know to what extent interdependencies motivate such large-team projects.
We address both social and epistemic questions using a large-scale bibliometric analysis of psychology publications.
We first examine how citation impact varies across team sizes, including citation counts within the first two years after publication.
We then extend previous work in two ways.

First, we compare researchers' own larger-and smaller-team publications, allowing us to examine whether the association between team size and citation impact is also apparent within individual researchers' publication records.

Second, we examine where the citation impact typical of larger-team papers falls within the citation distribution of smaller-team papers, providing a distributional perspective on the magnitude of these differences.

Finally, we examine whether larger-and smaller-team papers differ in the citation prestige of the journals in which they are published, both across papers and within individual researchers' publication records.
We complement these analyses by qualitatively examining the types of projects for which psychologists form large teams and the reasons for coordination at this scale.

Guided by the conceptual model of Rasti et al. (2026) we investigate whether coordination arises from logistic, financial, temporal, or epistemic interdependencies, while also identifying motivations that extend beyond these practical requirements.

(2026)</ref> we investigate whether coordination arises from logistic, financial, temporal, or epistemic interdependencies, while also identifying motivations that extend beyond these practical requirements.

text.text: This analysis clarifies when large-scale coordination is currently perceived as necessary or desirable.

text.text: OpenAlex is an open-access scholarly metadata resource launched in 2022 as a successor to Microsoft Academic Graph.
All data processing and analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.1 and higher, R Core Team, 2025).
OpenAlex stores all scholarly documents including journal articles within the works entity.
We iterated over the snapshot's works section and retrieved all entries in which Psychology or Decision Science appeared as the primary or secondary field.

Field assignment in OpenAlex is largely automated: a large language model (LLM) infers topics from the title, abstract, journal name, and citation network, and then maps topics to the most likely field using an algorithm developed by CWTS (OpenAlex, 2024).

text.text: Data Cleaning Process Note: Retrieving the OpenAlex data from the secondary field of papers introduced noise into the dataset.
The LLM model OpenAlex has used to categorise papers to fields is less accurate for the secondary field.
As a consequence, we screened the data at multiple stages and developed keyword-based rules to improve the efficiency of dataset cleaning.
The sample size for the first screening stage was chosen pragmatically and was further complemented by the random checks as part of the qualitative analysis.
The keywords identified during manual screening were used to develop systematic filtering rules for the dataset.
As individual keywords could match multiple records, we could identify a larger number of potentially irrelevant records.
Where keyword-based filtering was insufficient to identify irrelevant records reliably, we used journal ISSNs or individual OpenAlex IDs to facilitate their removal.
More information about data cleaning can be found in the supplementary material and in the code file r_scripts/02_data_cleaning.R available in the paper's repository.
To measure citation impact, we use (a) total citation counts, (b) second-year citation counts, and (c) publication-date-corrected citation counts.
We chose not to adjust for selfcitations for two reasons.
First, we lacked reliable self-citation data for all papers in the dataset.

Second, based on our own prior observations, large-team papers often bring together many of the field's active scholars (e.g., ManyPrimates) and produce results that serve as reference points for an entire research line.
Discounting self-citations would therefore risk understating the field-level impact that is central to the current study.
However, we tested the impact of self-citation on a subset of the data.

In this document, analyses use second-year citation counts; robustness analyses with the other metrics (i.e., total citation and publication-date-corrected citation) are reported in the Supplementary Materials.
We operationalized the impact of journals using the SCImago Journal Rank (SJR).

SJR is an open-access journal-ranking metric based on the citation impact of papers published in a journal, similar to other widely used journal-level metrics such as the Journal Impact Factor, but offers broader coverage (31,125 journals vs. 22,249 journals in Web of Science).
SJR divides all citations to a journal by all documents published by the journal over a specific time window.
Unlike the Impact Factor, SJR weighs citations by the prestige of the citing journal, which is estimated via a PageRank algorithm on the journal citation network, and discounts self-citations.
Although excluding self-citations may underestimate a journal's true prestige, we relied on SJR because we could not identify alternative open-access metrics that capture journals' ranking.
For comparison, in 2024, Nature had an Impact Factor of 48.5 and an SJR of 18.288 and Psychological Science had an Impact Factor of 5.1 and an SJR of 2.5.
Despite greater coverage, only 1177572 records in our dataset had matching journals in the SJR records.
Therefore, all results based on journal prestige are based on this subset.
In this paper, we did not impose a single threshold for large-team papers.
Wherever possible, we analyzed the full distribution of the number of co-authors.
We grouped papers into single-, two-, three-, four-, and five-author papers, and for the remaining papers we exploratively analyzed alternative bin widths of 5, 10, and 15 authors.
In each team-size bin, the final bin captured very large teams (>100 authors); except for the 10-author scheme, where the last bin began at ≥ 96 authors to preserve 10-author intervals.

text.text: In the remainder of this document, we report results using a bin width of 10 authors; robustness checks with other team size definitions are provided in the Supplementary Materials and reveal that bin size does not matter for the main conclusions.
We randomly selected 1000 papers with 20 or more authors for our qualitative analysis of the types of interdependencies that motivate researchers to collaborate.

We chose 20 as the cutoff for large-team projects because pairwise comparisons of citation counts showed that papers with more than 20 authors have consistently higher mean citation ranks than papers by smaller teams (see Supplementary Materials).
Our goal was to code 500 valid records, while at the same time using the qualitative checks to identify papers that did not meet the inclusion criteria of this study.
We analyzed 669 papers in total using MAXQDA 2022 software for the first round (version 22.1.0, VERBI Software, 2021) AND Microsoft Excel in the final round.
From the 169 papers that did not meet the inclusion criteria, we distilled keywords that were used in the second round of data cleaning (see Figure 1).

text.text: We used a combined deductive and inductive coding approach.
The initial codebook was informed by the four types of interdependence identified by Rasti et al. (2026): logistic, financial, temporal, and epistemic interdependencies.
text.formatted: The initial codebook was informed by the four types of interdependence identified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Rasti et al. (2026)</ref>: logistic, financial, temporal, and epistemic interdependencies.

text.text: During an initial round of coding, we allowed additional reasons for large-team collaboration that were not adequately captured by these predefined categories to emerge from the data.
The authors iteratively discussed these cases and refined the definitions, inclusion criteria, and examples associated with each code until consensus on the final codebook was reached.
Previously coded papers were subsequently reassessed using the final codebook.
Papers could receive more than one interdependency; however, interdependency codes and codes reflecting additional reasons for collaboration were mutually exclusive.
To assess coding reliability, the second and third authors each independently coded a randomly selected 10% of the final sample (50 papers each; 100 papers in total) using the final codebook.
After the first batch of 50 papers, inter-coder reliability was checked.
Reliability can be computed in two ways.
Per criterion (e.g., did both coders assign or not assign the category 'logistic').
Although in some categories the agreement was more than 90%, the mean agreement across all categories was 70.29 percent.

The second calculation can be based on whether each coder assigned exactly the same set of categories (e.g., both coders assign 'logistic', 'financial', and 'epistemic'), where the agreement was quite low at 32 percent.
We, therefore, adjusted the codebook and specified rules for all categories in more detail.
The second batch was coded afterward with the finalized codebook and led to the mean inter-coder agreement of 83.43 percent for criterion agreement and 60 percent for all-category agreement.
The main reason for imperfect agreement was unclear reporting in the papers, which required coders to make assumptions.
Disagreements, all of which involved edge cases, were discussed among the authors and resolved through consensus.
Following the reliability assessment, the first author coded the remainder of the sample using the finalized codebook.
More details on reliability assessment and agreement at the code level are available in the Supplementary Materials.
Coding was primarily based on the abstracts.

Coders additionally consulted the Methods section when 1) the abstract provided evidence for only one code, to determine whether any forms of interdependence were evident elsewhere in the paper; 2) it was unclear whether the study involved original data collection or re-analysis of existing data; or 3) the sample size could not be determined from the abstract.
For cases with no clear reason for large-team collaboration, the author-contribution statement was also consulted when available.

text.text: Among the four types of interdependency, logistic and financial interdependencies were the most frequent, identified in 295 and 225 papers, respectively.
Logistic and financial interdependencies often co-occur (i.e., in 105 papers) because collecting large sample sizes often combines both.

Papers were coded as involving logistic interdependency when they involved data collection across multiple sites; resource-intensive data collection (e.g., fMRI or data collection from primates); systematic reviews with more than 100 papers at the screening stage; secondary analyses combining data from multiple sources; or bibliometric and meta-scientific analyses with samples substantially larger than is typical for such research.
Financial interdependency primarily captured studies in which the required sample size was sufficiently large to make the project resource-intensive.

For quantitative research, this included studies with more than 100 participants from non-general populations (e.g., people with specific disorders), more than 1,000 participants from general populations in online studies, or more than 200 participants from general populations in in-person studies.
For qualitative studies, we used a threshold of 100 participants.
These numbers were selected arbitrarily and based on authors' expectations of the sample sizes within the field.
Selecting a threshold, despite its limitations, was necessary as it helped to resolve discrepancies that existed in the earlier version of the qualitative analysis.
Epistemic (111 papers) and temporal (92 papers) interdependencies were less frequent.

Epistemic interdependencies included complex clinical trials requiring expertise beyond what would typically be available to a single researcher; explicitly multidisciplinary research, or other research projects requiring multiple domains of specialized knowledge (e.g., combining physiological and psychological interventions); skills requiring extensive training (more than four years; e.g., conducting diagnostic interviews); and the development of research tools or the proposal or revision of guidelines.

Papers were coded as involving temporal interdependency when they included multiple data-collection time points (e.g., cohort or longitudinal studies and randomized controlled trials with follow-ups at least 3 months apart), multistage consensus development, or multiple sequential research stages within the same paper, such as developing and testing an instrument or conducting an original study and its replication.
Importantly, our categories were designed to capture interdependencies that could be identified from a single published paper.

Consequently, our temporal category captures somewhat different cases from those described by Rasti et al. (2026), because temporally interdependent stages of a research project do not necessarily appear within the same publication.
We also identified a category of papers that were part of a larger coordinated study or consortium.
These papers typically reported secondary analyses of data previously collected as part of a single cohort or a larger randomized controlled trial.
Large and complex studies can produce datasets with substantial informational value that can subsequently be used to address research questions beyond those examined in the original study.

However, as it was not always possible to determine the extent to which the interdependencies involved in the original study were inherited by the secondary analysis, we kept these papers as a separate category.
Large teams were also present in papers for which we could not identify the types of research interdependency described above.
One category comprised papers in which the large number of authors appeared primarily to serve a consensus or signalling function rather than to enable resource-intensive empirical research.
These included position papers, perspective pieces, commentaries, non-systematic reviews, event or workshop reports, and papers proposing research roadmaps.
In such papers, the inclusion of many authors may indicate broad support for a position, consensus around a perspective, or representation of a larger research community.
We therefore classified these papers separately.
Finally, in a small number of cases, we could not identify a clear reason for the inclusion of more than 20 authors.
These papers did not meet the criteria for any of the other categories, and the Methods and, where available, author-contribution statements did not provide further clarification.
This does not necessarily imply that no interdependencies were present.

It is possible that financial, logistic, temporal, or epistemic interdependencies existed, but they were not clearly enough communicated in the published paper to be identified using our coding procedure.

Alternatively, norms of a specific field may require the inclusion of all members of a group, rather than only those who directly contributed to the paper, which may be the case for some of the papers in this category.

Although larger teams publish papers that are on average cited more often, papers by smaller teams can also have high impact, and some of the highest impact papers are written by small teams.
However, the probability that papers written by small teams have high impact is low.

To explore the probability that a small team produces a paper with more impact than a large team, we examined the maximum number of citations after 2 years at the 70th, 80th, 90th, and 99th percentile.

Given that the mean and median second-year citations for papers with 20 authors or more are 28.84 and 4, respectively, Figure 6 shows that to have a chance to outperform the median second-year citation of larger author papers, small teams have to be at the top 19.61st percentile.

The same is true for the journal rank score but to a lesser extent.
To beat the median SJR value of larger teams (1.41), smaller team papers should be at the top 25.98th percentile.
In other words, although smaller-team papers can achieve greater citation impact than the median larger-team paper, only a relatively small proportion do so.
From an individual researcher's perspective, large-team papers tend to achieve recognition levels that smaller-team papers reach only at the highest end of their performance.

text.text: Total citation and second-year citation counts across qualitative categories with overlap
Coordination is essential to address complex research questions in science.
In response, many disciplines have increasingly organized themselves into larger research teams.

Within psychology in particular, the growing culture of team science raises important questions about how such work is evaluated within existing reward structures, and whether these incentives support or discourage further growth in team-based research.
This paper examined multiple aspects of the performance and impact of large-team papers in comparison to papers by small teams.
We also provided a qualitative investigation of the underlying motivations for why researchers work in large teams in scientific papers.

In line with previous work, we found that large-team papers have been increasing in number, receive higher citation counts, and are published in higher ranked journals (Coles, 2024; Coles et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2019; Wuchty et al., 2007).
text.formatted: In line with previous work, we found that large-team papers have been increasing in number, receive higher citation counts, and are published in higher ranked journals <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Coles, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Coles et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Wu et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Wuchty et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Although such papers still represent a minority of all publications, their growth may partly reflect the shift in topics that attract researchers and journal editors in psychology.
These projects can also offer researchers opportunities to work collaboratively, an aspect of academic research that many researchers value, and to expand their professional networks.

It may also be due to an increased expectation from scientists to excel at skills like self-awareness, communication, and project management (Bennett & Gadlin, 2012), which could, in principle, encourage researchers to participate in larger team projects as a way to learn and apply these skills.
text.formatted: It may also be due to an increased expectation from scientists to excel at skills like self-awareness, communication, and project management <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bennett & Gadlin, 2012)</ref>, which could, in principle, encourage researchers to participate in larger team projects as a way to learn and apply these skills.

text.text: It is important to consider the context in which citation metrics are interpreted.

Within the current academic reward structure, individual-level indicators such as citation counts, publications in highly ranked journals, and the rapid recognition of a researcher's work can influence career advancement (see Goring et al., 2014; Tiokhin et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Within the current academic reward structure, individual-level indicators such as citation counts, publications in highly ranked journals, and the rapid recognition of a researcher's work can influence career advancement (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Goring et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Tiokhin et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: One reason for relying on such indicators may be that scientific quality is a complex and difficult concept to assess directly, highlighting the need for continued discussion about what constitutes quality and how it should be evaluated.
Focusing on citation impact, our findings suggest that large-team papers tend to perform better than smaller-team papers.
This raises a question about whether these indicators adequately capture contributions that are valuable to science and whether researchers should be incentivized to pursue them.

This is a difficult discussion, as citations are correlated with scientific impact, but only as a proxy, and scientific research should not only have scientific, but also societal impact (for a discussion, see Isager et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This is a difficult discussion, as citations are correlated with scientific impact, but only as a proxy, and scientific research should not only have scientific, but also societal impact (for a discussion, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Isager et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The extent to which citations should be valued is a complex discussion, but in general, scientists, funders, and scientific organizations currently assign some value to citations when evaluating the scientific contribution of scientists.
As long as hiring, promotion, funding, and professional recognition continue to depend partly on citation metrics, researchers have incentives to perform well on them.
The value of citation impact and journal prestige may also differ across career stages.

Early-career researchers face particular pressure to establish themselves as independent scholars and develop a recognizable research profile (Bennett & Gadlin, 2012; Coles et al., 2022; Zucker, 2012).
text.formatted: Early-career researchers face particular pressure to establish themselves as independent scholars and develop a recognizable research profile <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bennett & Gadlin, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Coles et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Zucker, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: They may therefore hesitate to participate in large-team projects if having their contribution embedded within a long author list makes their individual contribution less visible, particularly when scientific credit is disproportionately attributed to principal investigators or other prominent contributors (Zucker, 2012).
text.formatted: They may therefore hesitate to participate in large-team projects if having their contribution embedded within a long author list makes their individual contribution less visible, particularly when scientific credit is disproportionately attributed to principal investigators or other prominent contributors <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Zucker, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This creates a potential tension between the benefits associated with large-team outputs and the visibility of an individual researcher's contribution to those outputs.
At the same time, early-career researchers may benefit from participating in large-team collaborations beyond having highly visible and highly cited publications.

For example, participation in such projects may provide new opportunities, expand professional networks, offer access to support and mentorship, and expose researchers to new scientific perspectives, skills, and expertise (Zucker, 2012).
text.formatted: For example, participation in such projects may provide new opportunities, expand professional networks, offer access to support and mentorship, and expose researchers to new scientific perspectives, skills, and expertise <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Zucker, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: It is uncertain how hiring committees, or committee members of research proposals should evaluate the contributions that researchers made on small-team papers compared to largeteam papers to appropriately recognize their scientific contributions.

Future research could examine how evaluators assess the CVs of early-career researchers with different combinations of small-and large-team publications, and whether these evaluations depend on citation impact, journal prestige, authorship position, or documented contributions.

Such work could help establish whether the potential benefits of large-team participation identified here translate into career advantages for individual researchers or whether concerns about diluted credit offset these benefits.

Narrative CVs, which allow scientists to describe the impact of their work, may provide evaluators with additional context and facilitate the recognition of a wider range of scientific contributions, such as contributions to team science.
The value of contributing to large-team projects may change once researchers have established an independent research profile.

At later career stages, large-team publications may provide additional opportunities for visibility and recognition, as more senior scientists might benefit more from demonstrating leadership ability than demonstrating independence.
Anecdotally, we have seen how authorship on a large-team paper that was published in a highly ranked journal increased a researcher's visibility within their institution.

Although these observations are anecdotal and should not be interpreted as evidence of a systematic career benefit, they illustrate one potential mechanism through which the citation and publication advantages associated with large-team research could translate into individual recognition.
More generally, these competing considerations suggest that the incentives and potential returns associated with participating in large-team science may vary substantially across career stages.
A limitation of our analysis is that our results focus on citation counts and journal rank, neither of which informs us directly about the quality of the scientific knowledge that is produced.
Moreover, it does not inform us about any possible causal mechanisms explaining the relationship between citation counts and team size.

Although we do not make claims about the quality of the studies or the mechanisms behind this relationship, a considerable body of work has cautioned that citation counts and journal visibility do not reliably reflect research quality (Aksnes et al., 2019; Dougherty & Horne, 2022; Seglen, 1997).
text.formatted: Although we do not make claims about the quality of the studies or the mechanisms behind this relationship, a considerable body of work has cautioned that citation counts and journal visibility do not reliably reflect research quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Aksnes et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Dougherty & Horne, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Seglen, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Several mechanisms can generate higher citation counts or publication in higher-ranked journals without necessarily reflecting differences in scientific quality.
For example, the broader relevance of topics addressed by larger collaborations may increase their visibility and, consequently, their citation counts (Wu et al., 2019).
text.formatted: For example, the broader relevance of topics addressed by larger collaborations may increase their visibility and, consequently, their citation counts <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Wu et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Citation patterns may also be affected by social and cognitive biases.

Large collaborations frequently include more prestigious researchers and institutions, are often led by researchers from higher-resource countries, and typically involve larger samples (Coles et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Large collaborations frequently include more prestigious researchers and institutions, are often led by researchers from higher-resource countries, and typically involve larger samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Coles et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These characteristics may trigger authority-related biases and increase citations independently of research quality (Urlings et al., 2021).
text.formatted: These characteristics may trigger authority-related biases and increase citations independently of research quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Urlings et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Citation counts may further be affected by self-citation (Aksnes, 2003), although the association between team size and citations has also been observed after accounting for self-citations in both our study and previous studies (e.g., Larivière et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Citation counts may further be affected by self-citation <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aksnes, 2003)</ref>, although the association between team size and citations has also been observed after accounting for self-citations in both our study and previous studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Larivière et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Network effects may also impact the citation count, as larger teams may have broader social and professional networks through which their work becomes visible and subsequently cited (Li et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Network effects may also impact the citation count, as larger teams may have broader social and professional networks through which their work becomes visible and subsequently cited <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Li et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: And indeed, our data extend these findings by showing how perspective and opinion pieces by large groups of authors gather a substantial number of citations.
Citation-based indicators are only one proxy for scientific impact.

Alternative indicators include references to research in patents, policy, legal, or other non-academic documents, as well as measures of online attention, such as the number of times an article is saved, shared, or discussed on social media (Beerdsen, 2025; Brown, 2014; Velayos-Ortega & López-Carreño, 2023).
text.formatted: Alternative indicators include references to research in patents, policy, legal, or other non-academic documents, as well as measures of online attention, such as the number of times an article is saved, shared, or discussed on social media <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Beerdsen, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brown, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Velayos-Ortega & López-Carreño, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, these measures capture different dimensions of research influence, and each measure comes with its own limitations.

Patent citations, for example, may be more informative in fields with direct technological applications and less generalizable to the social sciences, while policy, legal, and clinical uptake represent qualitatively different forms of societal influence that are difficult to combine into a single measure.
Measures of online attention similarly capture visibility or engagement rather than necessarily reflecting research quality.
Throughout this paper, we interpret citation counts specifically as an indicator of citation impact and SJR as an indicator of journal-level citation prestige.

Our findings should be interpreted as evidence that large-team papers tend to receive greater scholarly citation attention and appear in journals with greater citation prestige, rather than evidence that large-team collaborations necessarily produce higher-quality science.
Through our qualitative analysis, we found that interdependencies were the most common reason for forming large teams.
Among these, logistic and financial interdependencies were particularly frequent, which is consistent with the findings of Coles et al. (2026).
text.formatted: Among these, logistic and financial interdependencies were particularly frequent, which is consistent with the findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Coles et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that scaling up research (for example, by collecting larger samples or collecting data across multiple sites) is an important reason for large-team collaboration.

This pattern may point to a mismatch between how research is conventionally organized and funded in psychology and the resources required to address increasingly ambitious research questions and methodological standards.

Research funding is still often organized around individual PIs and their research groups and focuses more on novelty rather than what is required for further developing knowledge generation (Vaesen, 2026).
text.formatted: Research funding is still often organized around individual PIs and their research groups and focuses more on novelty rather than what is required for further developing knowledge generation <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Vaesen, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, researchers are expected to meet standards that require resources that exceed the capacity of a single investigator or laboratory.

Large-team collaboration may provide one way of addressing this mismatch by pooling financial resources, infrastructure, access to participants, and scientific labour across researchers and institutions.
In doing so, large teams may also make methodologically demanding research designs feasible by distributing the labour and resources required to implement them.
Our results also showed that the infrastructure created through large-team coordination can remain valuable beyond the project for which it was initially established.
By establishing shared datasets, methodological standards, collaborative networks, and data-sharing mechanisms, large teams can create resources that can support future research.
This was apparent in papers from our sample that relied on secondary analyses of data generated through large cohorts, clinical trials, or consortia.

Although the analyses in these papers may not have necessarily required the same interdependencies as the original data collection, they relied on data that could only have been generated through substantial coordination.
The scientific value of large-team coordination extends beyond its immediate outputs, with datasets and protocols providing resources for subsequent research.

This also raises questions about co-authorship, as the data shared by large collaborations is often valuable for other scientific contributions, and was often collected at substantial financial or logistical costs.

If subsequent research depends on the investments of a large collaboration, it might be important for fields to reflect on how they provide credit for the work that went into generating these rich datasets.
We also found that large teams can serve functions beyond addressing the interdependencies associated with complex empirical research.
For example, some large-team publications in our sample were position papers, perspectives, commentaries, workshop reports, or research roadmaps.

In these cases, the large number of authors may serve a signaling function, indicating broad support for a position, drawing attention to an issue, or representing consensus across a research community.
These functions are not necessarily problematic.
Establishing consensus and research priorities are important steps in scientific coordination (Rasti et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Establishing consensus and research priorities are important steps in scientific coordination <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Rasti et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A smaller subset of the papers we investigated did not reveal an apparent reason for the large number of authors.
These categories raise questions about how individual contributions are defined and communicated.
This may be due to social reasons for collaborations, such as benefiting from the increased visibility of the output, as mentioned by Jones (2021).
text.formatted: This may be due to social reasons for collaborations, such as benefiting from the increased visibility of the output, as mentioned by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Jones (2021)</ref>.

text.text: It may also be a sign of honorary or gift authorship, which has been shown to occur in science (Gülen et al., 2020).
text.formatted: It may also be a sign of honorary or gift authorship, which has been shown to occur in science <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Gülen et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A CRediT statement might help to transparently specify contributions of each author and prevent the impression of gift authorship.

However, relatively broad categories in a CRediT statement do not necessarily communicate the magnitude or importance of each contribution, or the extent to which a particular contribution was necessary for the research.

Research communities may therefore need to consider whether existing authorship conventions adequately distinguish between authorship reflecting direct contributions to a specific scholarly output and participation intended primarily to signal collective endorsement.
As long as recognition and reward procedures remain focused on individuals, improving coordination in science requires that the benefits of collaborative work be tangible for individual researchers.

Our findings suggest that large-team collaborations are more likely to receive citation impact and visibility, often generate more immediate influence, and are on average cited more and published in higher-ranked journals than small-team papers by the same author.

Moreover, this study highlights that large-team collaborations primarily arise from the interdependencies and demands of complex research questions, but also from broader social and strategic factors.

While coordinated research should ideally be driven by intrinsic scientific goals, making these additional motivators explicit may help increase the adoption of coordinated large-team research in scientific disciplines such as psychology.
We need coordination to answer complex questions, and our results show that coordination is potentially rewarding in the current state of academia.
